name: prioritization
context: An agent confronts a backlog larger than the compute available to it: a queue of issues, tickets, documents, search results, or subtasks where finishing everything in this turn is impossible. A priority layer sits in front of the executor loop and decides which pending item runs next, and it re-decides rather than fixing the order once. Two things make this distinct from routing (routing classifies an input and dispatches it to a handler, one-shot, and does not model contention) and from a step budget (a step budget caps how much an agent spends, it does not choose what it spends it on). The ordering signal is typically a composite: an explicit business priority (Critical > High > Normal > Low), an estimated token cost so that short jobs drain first under shortest-job-first, a dependency gate so a task is not eligible until its predecessors in a DAG complete, and a recency or dependency-derived re-rank after each completion. Re-prioritization matters because new information changes the ranking: a task whose result revealed an urgent blocker, or one that turned out to be infeasible, should move immediately rather than at the next planning cycle. The pattern applies both to a single agent managing its own queue (create -> execute -> re-prioritize, the BabyAGI loop) and to a serving layer multiplexing many concurrent agents onto a fixed pool of model capacity, where the queue is the contention point and starvation of high-value work is the failure mode being fixed.
benefits: Spends a fixed token or time budget on the highest-value pending work instead of draining the queue in arrival order
Prevents starvation: a continuously-refreshed priority order bounds the wait of a high-priority task even under sustained load of low-priority work
Shortest-job-first within a priority class raises aggregate throughput because long jobs do not block a backlog of cheap ones
A dependency gate makes execution order correct rather than merely cheap, so a task never runs before its inputs exist
Re-prioritization after each completion turns execution results into scheduling information, which a one-shot classifier cannot use
tradeoffs: Cost estimation is the weak link: ranking by a mis-estimated token cost degrades scheduling to arrival order, and LLM-based cost prediction is itself noisy
A stale priority list is worse than none, because the agent commits to a now-wrong order; priorities must be recomputed after every completion or bounded staleness must be enforced
Adds a model call per re-rank on top of the execution call, which is a real tax on cheap tasks and can be self-defeating at high queue depth
Priority inversion still occurs at the boundary: the layer can only reorder what has already been admitted, so a genuinely urgent task arriving behind a large admitted batch waits for the batch
Shared static priority classes are a policy artifact, not a fact about the work, and encode the priorities of whoever set them; they can systematically devalue long-running or low-visibility work
use_cases: A coding agent working a backlog of issues under a per-run token budget, skipping items it judges infeasible and re-ranking the rest after each completion
A SOC alert triage agent ordering queued incidents by blast radius while dependencies on evidence-gathering steps gate eligibility
A research agent holding a sub-question queue and reordering it as retrieval reveals which questions are already answered and which are blocking
A serving proxy multiplexing many concurrent agents onto a fixed RPM/TPM pool, prioritizing by task class so that a low-value backlog cannot starve an interactive session
avoid_when: The queue always fits within the budget, in which case ordering is a no-op and the extra re-rank call is pure overhead
The work is latency-critical and interactive, where any scheduling indirection is felt directly as tail latency
A single user is waiting on one answer, since there is nothing to prioritize against
Priority cannot be estimated better than arrival order, in which case the layer adds a model call and buys nothing
component_types: priority queue with re-rank on completion
cost estimator for expected token spend
executor loop consuming one item at a time
anti_patterns: Fixing the priority order once at plan time and then executing it literally, so execution results cannot influence scheduling
Ranking purely by an LLM's stated difficulty or importance rather than by an estimated cost or dependency signal, which is uncorrelated with actual token spend
Letting every queued task be simultaneously eligible, so a cheap task with no dependencies queues behind an expensive blocking one
Re-ranking on every loop iteration even when no new information arrived, spending more on scheduling than on work
Using a shared priority class as a proxy for urgency without recording who assigned it, so the ranking is unauditable
design_principles: Re-rank on state change, not on a timer, so scheduling cost is paid only when it can change the decision
Separate eligibility (dependencies satisfied) from ordering (value and cost), so a correct dependency graph is not entangled with a heuristic ranking
Bound priority staleness explicitly, because a stale rank is an ordering decision made on evidence that no longer holds
Make the ordering signal auditable, since a priority that cannot be explained cannot be contested or corrected
Treat the queue as the contention point; contention is what makes ordering a pattern rather than a nicety
best_practices: Order by (explicit priority class, estimated cost, arrival time) so that the intent-bearing signal dominates and cost only breaks ties within a class
Track dependency edges as a DAG with cycle detection and gate eligibility on predecessor completion
Refresh the rank after each completion and after any failure that changes the feasibility of remaining work
Log the priority, the rank, and the reason for each promotion or demotion so reordering is reviewable
Measure scheduling overhead as a fraction of total token spend and drop the layer when it exceeds the value it returns
Enforce starvation bounds by aging, so a task cannot sit below a fixed priority indefinitely no matter how much lower-value work arrives
